https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn7n.text: Figure caption, Watch: Israeli settlers return to settlement of Kadim By Lucy Williamson Middle East Correspondent ,Â Reporting from Jenin Published 21 August 2026, 06:00 BST A new generation of Israeli settlers has returned to the settlement of Kadim, in the occupied West Bank, two decades after it was closed by a previous Israeli government. Thirty "pioneer families" had arrived in the settlement on Thursday from Tel Aviv, according to the regional settlers' council, riding a wave of Jewish nationalism driven by Israel's current government. They came in small groups, some under military escort, blue and white Israeli flags fluttering from their cars as they passed Palestinian villages and farmlands. Some dragged trailers loaded with bedding, furniture and building material. Israel's government has overturned a 20-year ban on Jewish settlements around Jenin. Palestinian residents are watching the new push on settlement expansion here with fear. All Israeli settlements and settler outposts are illegal under international law. Outposts are also illegal under Israeli law, though are often supported by state services and funding. "21 years after the crime of expulsion from northern Samaria, we have completed the correction [â¦] and have returned to the settlement of Kadim," said Israel's far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich at the opening ceremony, using the Biblical word for the northern West Bank. Israel opens up bids for highly sensitive West Bank settlement project Published 1 day ago The West Bank settler siege Israeli West Bank settler tells BBC attacks on Palestinians are justified as revenge Published 1 August Alongside him were Israel's Justice Minister, the Speaker of the Knesset, and Yossi Dagan, head of the regional settlers' council, who vowed that settlers would one day return to Gaza too. Kadim, on a small hillside outside the Palestinian city of Jenin , was evacuated in 2005 by a previous Israeli government as part of a wider unilateral Disengagement Plan that also saw all Jewish settlers and soldiers pulled out of Gaza, and three other settlements in the northern West Bank dismantled. At the time, the four settlements were considered too isolated and costly to protect, and of little strategic value. Image caption, Senior Israeli politicians including Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana attended a national ceremony In recent weeks, white trailer homes have appeared on the hilltop here again, in preparation for families to return. Our request to speak to people at the opening ceremony was refused; we were told no media were allowed to enter the settlement today. Driving along a dirt track on the hill behind it, we met a Palestinian vegetable farmer, living in the house he was born in 53 years ago. He told me how, as a boy, he watched Kadim being built for the first time, then watched again as the settlers there were forced out by the government twenty years later. "Back then, the settlers were living alongside us, and we coexisted peacefully. They lived their lives and we lived ours," he told me. Now, watching them return, he's fearful. "I'm afraid of the events spreading around us, and the bypass road [where] they demolished shops and businesses," he said. "They drove my nephews away from their vegetables and citrus trees, telling them 'you have no place here, don't come back'". He said his family fled here from Haifa during the 1948 Arab-Israeli War. "There's no more displacement left in me," he said. "We're living with a sense of resignation. It's a life of fear." After Kadim and the three other settlements here were evacuated in 2005, Israelis were banned from settling in this area. Israel's current government overturned that ban. Kadim is the last of the settlements evacuated in 2005 to reopen. Ganim, Sanur and Homesh have already been formally opened, and families moved in. But they are a drop in the ocean of the Israeli government's settlement project here. Since it took power in late 2022, it has approved more than 100 new settlements across the West Bank, including 19 in the northern West Bank. Hagit Ofran, director of the Settlement Watch programme at Peace Now, says the rapid construction in Jenin is part of a wider race by the Israeli government to expand settlements in the West Bank before Israeli elections are held in October. One of those new settlements is Emek Dotan, to the west of Jenin, formally opened last Sunday and now home to almost two dozen Jewish families. From the small hamlet of Palestinian houses next door to Emek Dotan, teacher Samer Jaber, has watched the settlement take shape: first the bulldozers, then the caravans lifted into place. The problems began even before most of the families moved in, he said. "Groups come and stand opposite our houses, filming us," he told me. "Yesterday they came and stood here, filming me and my children. Every time my wife stepped outside, they filmed her too. They try to enter our homes. And they go house by house, shining powerful floodlights directly through all the windows at two or three in the morning." Image caption, Problems began even before most of the families moved in, schoolteacher Samer Jaber told the BBC Samer is partially blind and has a leg injury that makes moving difficult. "Fear dominates everything. We are completely defenceless," he said. "All of them have weapons. I'm bringing concrete blocks to close off this side of the house because I'm afraid for my children." Samer has watched settlements â and settler attacks â grow in other parts of the West Bank over the past few years, despite international pressure. "Europe has no time for us, America is preoccupied with Iran, China has no interest," his analysis began. "Russia is busy with Ukraine, the United Nations is finished, and the Arab countries have their own internal problems." "Democratic systems are over, they're finished," he concluded, anger and bitterness leaking out. "Civilisation, progress and modernity are lies." Alongside the new settlements around Jenin, two new Israeli military bases are rapidly going up â construction vehicles churning up dust behind high concrete walls topped with watchtowers and barbed wire, Israeli flags flapping in the wind. A military outpost is also being built on seized Palestinian land beside Jenin Refugee Camp â the first Israeli military base to be built on land under full Palestinian Authority control since the Oslo Accords were signed in 1993. Israel's military evacuated thousands of residents from Jenin Refugee camp before occupying it in 2025. The Israel Defence Forces confirmed that construction of the outpost in Jabriyat had been ordered "in accordance with operational needs". The Palestinian Authority Governor for Jenin, Kamal Abu al-Rub, told me he was worried that Israel's seizure of land around the refugee camp signalled a plan to house settlers there, right in the heart of a Palestinian city, dividing it up like Hebron or Jerusalem. He described the past two decades without settlers around Jenin as "bliss". "Now, we live in the hell orchestrated by them and their assaults," he said. "It limits our movement. They cut off roads, bulldoze lands and cut down trees." The speed of change here is breathtaking. A few weeks ago, I sat drinking coffee in a cafÃ© on the road that runs from Kadim through the northern West Bank to Israel: now that cafÃ© â and dozens of Palestinian shops and businesses around it â are just piles of rubble along the road; demolished by the Israeli army. The countdown to Israeli elections in October marked in the number of Palestinian buildings demolished, the number of new settler caravans. https://www.politico.eu/article/meet-the.text: BRUSSELS — The Greens in the European Parliament will on Tuesday pick new leaders, as the group seeks to reverse its waning influence amid Europe’s rightward shift and launch a comeback in the 2029 EU election. The vote is part of the Parliament’s midterm reshuffle, with a host of top posts up for grabs. The Greens are voting now because Bas Eickhout resigned in May as leader of the group and as an MEP amid revelations of undisclosed relationships with staffers. Eickhout was not only the face of the Greens in the Parliament, but also one of the best-known MEPs in Brussels and in his native Netherlands. With other group leaders expected to stay in post — or with succession deals already struck — the Green vote is likely to be the reshuffle’s only open leadership race, and as has long been the case, they’ll pick two co-chairs. The candidates are working the phones and going office-to-office to secure the backing of the group’s 53 lawmakers (the Greens are the sixth-largest group in the Parliament). Advertisement Advertisement All four broadly back a shift from pragmatic dealmaking inside the Parliament toward more offensive mobilization, gearing up for a 2029 EU election in which they hope to reverse heavy losses in 2024 , and getting lawmakers out of Parliament and onto the streets. POLITICO spoke to all the candidates. The vote takes place on Tuesday, with a press conference scheduled for 6.15 p.m. to announce the winners. Terry Reintke — the continuity candidate Germany’s Reintke has helped lead the group since 2022 and is widely expected to win one of the two co-chair posts. “I’m quite optimistic, quite confident,” she said in an interview. Reintke says she believes the Greens can exert influence through pragmatic dealmaking, but also wants to take a more assertive approach. Terry Reintke takes part in a vote during a plennary session at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France on May 20, 2026. | Sebastien Bozon/AFP via Getty Images The group “is really longing to focus more on external communication … to be more outspoken, to be more with the people, to go more outside of the European Parliament, to be more on the ground,” she said, adding that “this is … a sort of politics that I come from, that I was raised with.” Such a change does not mean removing the Greens from the majority that supports the Commission, Reintke argued. Despite its rightward shift and rollback of green policies, the group can still secure wins by negotiating, she said, citing as an example the EU’s 2040 climate target, which falls short of Green ambitions but remains in place. Advertisement Advertisement “I think this is going to stay,” she said of the pragmatic dealmaking. On some occasions, however, when the group considers it can’t win anything from a deal, “we are ready to also go into oppositional mode.” That captures the tension shaping the race. Some national delegations within the Greens favor compromise and continued support for Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, while others want a tougher stance against her executive, which is dominated by the conservative European People’s Party. Nicolae Ștefănuță — the grassroots newcomer Ștefănuță joined the Greens in 2023 after defecting from the liberals. He ran as an independent in the 2024 EU election, gathering more than 100,000 signatures urging him to stand and 300,000 votes, according to his pitch for the leadership. He has put that grassroots success at the heart of his bid. Nicolae Ștefănuță is pictured at an exhibition at the European Parliament, in Strasbourg, on Nov. 25, 2025. | Magali Cohen/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images “I have this special expertise in winning, in doing modern campaigns that we need to do in Europe to fight off the far-right,” he said. He is also playing the geographic-balance card as the group’s eastern and southern wings seek a more diverse leadership. “I’m from the East and I’ve been … working with everybody, no matter what the region,” he said. “I have a confidence to really build bridges between all the members of the group and be really a uniter.” Advertisement Advertisement Like Reintke, Ștefănuță says the Greens should strike deals where possible. “I don’t believe in automatic opposition,” he told POLITICO. He is courting smaller delegations by promising to give them a greater voice and prevent the priorities of larger national groups from dominating. “I am also running against the idea of maintaining the status quo. We have not always done things right. We should not be complacent,” he wrote in his email pitch to fellow MEPs, in an apparent dig at previous leadership. “We have not always treated everyone with understanding. The 13 one-person delegations of this group sometimes feel lonely. Instead of asking what they deliver, why don’t we ask what they need? How can we help you?” he wrote. Isabella Lövin — the former minister Lövin is selling experience, reliability and a network she says can help shape EU policy. She served as Sweden’s international development minister, environment minister and deputy prime minister between 2016 and 2021, after a stint as an MEP from 2009 to 2014. Advertisement Advertisement Her goal for the next two-and-a-half years “is to make the Greens as relevant as possible” to fight the far right and put Europe back on “a course” toward sustainability, reduced inequality and less dependence on fossil fuels. “We should never give up on trying to influence the legislative work,” she said, while also becoming “more vocal on issues which really are understandable to our voters.” Her experience among EU ministers “could also open a few doors to have us [be] more relevant in discussions,” she said. “I have a very extensive network throughout Europe, all colleagues, both green and not green, to try to kind of … navigate these very, very stormy waters and make us relevant through that.” Isabella Lövin is selling experience, reliability and a network she says can help shape EU policy. | Martin Bertrand/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images Lövin said her profile complements Reintke’s activist and grassroots links, and she expects Reintke to be reelected. Together, they “can cover many areas and speak to different audiences,” she said. She acknowledged divisions over how pragmatic versus oppositional the Greens should be, and said the group should allow each delegation to do what’s best in a national context. “My leadership style is always to listen to everyone and try to find a good joint idea about how to go forward,” she said. “We should focus more on how to communicate and to help smaller delegations to communicate back home.” Advertisement Advertisement Sara Matthieu — the policy hand Flemish MEP Matthieu casts herself as both a grassroots campaigner and pragmatic dealmaker with extensive policy expertise — pitched somewhere between Ștefănuță and Lövin. Inside Parliament, Matthieu says the Greens must stand their ground and be “super clear” on issues such as further environmental rollbacks. “I do think we need to be clearer in some of those battles, where we really have to say, ‘guys, now as a Commission, but also as a Parliament, you are taking it too far. This is really not acceptable anymore.’” Sara Matthieu participates in a plenary session of the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Sept. 15, 2026. | Philippe Buissin/European Parliament At the same time, the Greens must keep pressing the Commission for results, she said, citing von der Leyen’s recent heat action plan as a product of the group’s “pressure.” “It’s not just the battle inside of the Parliament that we need to win, it’s also outside. It’s out on the streets and it’s conquering people’s hearts with the message.” “For the last two-and-a-half years, we have been the adults in the room, holding the center together while the EPP had no problem relying on far-right majorities to get its way. We did a lot of damage control against this Commission’s reckless deregulation agenda. With me as co-president, we will shift our priorities,” she wrote in her program sent to fellow lawmakers. Advertisement Matthieu wants the Greens on the streets, joining citizens’ protests across the EU, but also in dialogue with “innovative business leaders,” workers and trade unions, spreading their message across Europe. She says her policy expertise and track record set her apart. She helped shape the group’s green industrial strategy and has taken a leading role in the Parliament’s environment committee (she was previously on the employment committee). Matthieu pointed to “a lot of knowledge on green policies, on climate policies, on protecting people’s health … that is something that sets me apart.”
